title: Chrome Renderer Sandbox
description: Chrome’s renderer sandbox is the reference implementation of browser isolation. Each tab’s renderer process — the code that parses HTML, runs JavaScript, and paints pixels — starts with a restricted token and job object on Windows, a seccomp-bpf filter plus namespaces on Linux, and a seatbelt sandbox profile on macOS. The renderer cannot open files, spawn processes, or touch the network; every privileged operation goes through IPC to the browser (broker) process, which validates the request against policy before acting. The sandbox’s strength is defense in depth: even with a renderer remote-code-execution bug, the attacker must then find a sandbox escape — a second, rarer bug — to reach the system. Chrome’s vulnerability rewards program prices this chain accordingly: renderer RCE plus sandbox escape earns the top tier. Site isolation completed the model by dedicating one renderer process per site, so a compromised renderer cannot even read another site’s data in memory.
key_points: Renderer runs restricted: no files, processes, or network
Broker validates every privileged request
RCE plus escape needed for system compromise
Site isolation: one process per site

title: Firefox Content Process Sandbox
description: Firefox’s sandbox (codenamed Electrolysis for the multi-process project) isolates web content in restricted child processes with levels the user can tune. On Windows, content processes run at low integrity with restricted tokens; on Linux, seccomp-bpf filters plus chroot-style filesystem restrictions; on macOS, seatbelt profiles. Firefox exposes the sandbox level in about:config (security.sandbox.content.level), letting users and enterprises trade compatibility for containment — higher levels break some plugins and DRM paths while shrinking the attack surface. The content process cannot read the profile directory directly; cookies, history, and passwords live in the parent process and are brokered on request. Firefox’s approach differs from Chrome’s mainly in configurability and in its process-per-tab-group model, but the security contract is identical: compromised content stays in its box. Mozilla treats sandbox escapes as critical (sec-critical) bugs with rapid chemspill releases.
key_points: Multi-process content isolation, tunable levels
Content cannot read the profile directory directly
about:config level trades compatibility for containment
Escapes rated sec-critical with rapid releases

title: Safari WebContent Sandbox
description: Safari’s WebContent sandbox reflects Apple’s platform philosophy: the OS vendor and the browser vendor are the same, so the sandbox integrates deeply with system frameworks. Each tab’s WebContent process runs under a seatbelt profile — Apple’s mandatory access control sandboxing — that whitelists exactly which files, Mach services, and network operations the renderer may touch. WebKit’s multi-process architecture (WebContent, Networking, GPU, UI processes) means even the network stack runs isolated from page content. On iOS the sandbox is stricter still: every app, including browsers (which must use WebKit), runs in its container, and just-in-time JavaScript compilation was historically restricted — a constraint that shaped mobile web performance for years. The Intelligent Tracking Prevention and Private Relay features run as further sandboxes around identity rather than code. Safari’s sandbox benefits from hardware integration — Pointer Authentication on ARM chips raises the cost of the memory-corruption bugs that precede escapes.
key_points: Seatbelt profiles whitelist files, services, network
Network stack isolated from page content
iOS: containers plus historical JIT restrictions
ARM Pointer Authentication raises exploit cost

title: Windows Sandbox (Disposable VM)
description: Windows Sandbox, shipped in Windows 10 Pro/Enterprise since 2019, is the disposable-VM answer to “should I run this file?” It spins up a lightweight virtual machine — a clean Windows install sharing the host’s kernel files via a dynamic base image — in seconds, gives you a pristine desktop, and throws the entire VM away when you close the window. Nothing persists: malware detonated inside cannot reach the host, and cannot survive the close. The integration is the clever part: the VM shares immutable system files with the host (memory pages shared, not copied), so it starts fast and costs little disk, while all writes go to the VM’s disposable overlay. Clipboard, file sharing, and networking are configurable — hardened users disable them for maximum isolation. It is not a performance environment (no vGPU by default, limited resources), but as a detonation chamber for email attachments and downloads, it is the best-built consumer sandbox in the industry.
key_points: Lightweight VM from a dynamic base image; seconds to start
Nothing persists — close the window, malware dies
Shares immutable host files; writes go to disposable overlay
Clipboard/network configurable for harder isolation

title: Qubes OS: Security by Compartmentalization
description: Qubes OS takes the sandbox to its logical extreme: the entire operating system is a set of isolated virtual machines. Every application domain — work, personal, banking, untrusted browsing — runs in its own qube (a lightweight Xen VM), color-coded by trust level, and compromise of one qube cannot reach the others or the dom0 management domain. Copy-paste and file transfer between qubes go through explicit, user-confirmed brokers. Disposable qubes extend the model: a fresh VM spun up for one risky document or link, destroyed afterward. The “disposable browser” workflow — every untrusted link opens in a fresh disposable qube — makes drive-by attacks nearly pointless. The cost is real: Qubes demands modern hardware with virtualization extensions, significant RAM, and a user willing to think in compartments. For journalists, activists, and security researchers facing targeted attacks, it is the strongest desktop posture available — security by architecture rather than by patching.
key_points: Whole OS as isolated Xen VMs per trust domain
Compromise of one qube cannot reach others or dom0
Disposable qubes: fresh VM per risky document
Demands hardware, RAM, and compartment thinking

title: SELinux and AppArmor: Mandatory Access Control
description: SELinux and AppArmor are Linux’s mandatory access control (MAC) systems — sandboxes enforced by the kernel regardless of what the application wants. SELinux (NSA-originated, default on RHEL/Fedora) labels every process, file, and port with a security context and enforces a system-wide policy: a compromised web server process running as httpd_t cannot read user home files even as root, because the policy — not Unix permissions — decides. AppArmor (default on Ubuntu/SUSE) takes the path-based approach: profiles list exactly which files each program may touch, written in readable syntax administrators can audit. Both confine even root processes — the historic weakness where “root exploit equals game over” becomes “root exploit equals confined attacker.” The reputation for difficulty is earned mainly by SELinux’s early tooling; modern setroubleshoot and permissive-mode workflows make policy development manageable. Containers, Android, and Flatpak all build on these primitives — MAC is the kernel bedrock under the user-friendly sandboxes.
key_points: Kernel-enforced policy regardless of app wishes
SELinux: label-based contexts; AppArmor: path profiles
Confines even root processes
Bedrock under containers, Android, Flatpak
t: SELinux and AppArmor: Mandatory Access Control

title: Firejail: Per-Application Linux Sandboxing
description: Firejail brings sandboxing to any Linux desktop application with one command: `firejail firefox` runs the browser with seccomp filters, network and mount namespaces, filesystem whitelists, and capability drops defined by a profile. Profiles ship for hundreds of applications — browsers, PDF readers, media players, chat clients — each tuned to the app’s legitimate needs: the PDF reader sees only the document you opened, the browser sees only its own config. The profile language is plain text and auditable, and users can tighten profiles further (no network for the PDF reader, read-only home for the editor). Firejail’s power is its incrementality: sandbox the risky apps today without re-architecting the system, unlike OS-wide MAC deployments. Limitations are honest: it relies on the same kernel primitives as everything else (a kernel exploit escapes it), and profiles need maintenance as applications change their file-access patterns. For the Linux user who wants Chrome-grade containment for arbitrary apps, it is the most practical tool available.
key_points: One command sandboxes any app: namespaces, seccomp, whitelists
Hundreds of shipped profiles, plain-text and auditable
Incremental: sandbox risky apps without system re-architecture
Profiles need maintenance as apps change

title: Flatpak and Snap: Packaged Sandboxes
description: Flatpak and Snap solve two problems at once — dependency hell and application isolation — by shipping apps with their runtimes inside kernel-enforced sandboxes. A Flatpak app runs in namespaces with no host filesystem visibility by default; it reaches user files only through portals — the file chooser portal hands it exactly the files you pick, the screenshot portal the pixels you approve. Permissions are declared in metadata and reviewable in tools like Flatseal, which lets users revoke network, device, or filesystem access per app. Snap (Ubuntu’s system) uses AppArmor profiles plus namespaces with a similar portal model. The sandbox improves on traditional packaging security dramatically: the distro-maintained app with full home-directory access is replaced by a publisher-maintained app that sees only what you grant. Criticisms are fair: many apps still request broad permissions (defeating the model), portal coverage has gaps, and duplicate runtimes cost disk. The trajectory is toward tighter defaults — the sandbox that ships permissive today enforces strictly tomorrow.
key_points: Apps ship with runtimes inside namespace sandboxes
Portals grant exactly the files you pick
Flatseal: per-app permission review and revocation
Many apps still over-request — defaults tightening over time

title: Android Application Sandbox
description: Android’s application sandbox is Linux user separation applied at scale: every installed app gets a unique UID, and the kernel’s discretionary access control makes each app’s private directory unreadable to every other app — no special framework needed, just Unix semantics. Inter-app communication goes through intents and content providers, each gated by permissions the user grants at runtime (camera, location, contacts) and can revoke anytime in settings. Since Android 6, permissions are runtime rather than install-time, and background access is progressively restricted — background location, for example, now requires explicit justification. SEAndroid (SELinux policies) adds mandatory access control confining even system processes. App integrity comes from signatures plus Play Protect scanning. The sandbox’s real-world record is strong: on unmodified devices with Play Store apps, malware overwhelmingly arrives through social engineering and sideloaded APKs, not sandbox escapes. Scoped storage (Android 10–12) closed the shared-external-storage loophole, giving each app only its own files plus media the user explicitly grants.
key_points: Per-app Linux UID: kernel-enforced file separation
Runtime permissions, revocable anytime
SEAndroid MAC confines even system processes
Scoped storage closed the shared-storage loophole

title: iOS App Sandbox and Entitlements
description: iOS runs the strictest consumer sandbox in wide deployment. Every app lives in its own container — a private directory the kernel denies to all other apps — and capabilities beyond the container come only as entitlements: cryptographic grants signed into the app’s provisioning profile by Apple (push notifications, iCloud, HealthKit, specific hardware). Shared resources are brokered: the photo picker hands the app only selected images, the document picker only chosen files — the app never browses the library itself. All executable code must be signed; dynamic code loading is restricted, and just-in-time compilation was long limited to WebKit — constraints that shaped the mobile web. Background execution is tightly lifecycle-managed, killing whole classes of spyware behavior. The sandbox’s strength is also its controversy: the same walls that contain malware enforce App Store exclusivity — security and platform control share the foundation. For the user, the practical result is the safest mainstream app ecosystem measured by in-the-wild malware rates.
key_points: Per-app containers; capabilities as signed entitlements
Brokered pickers: apps receive only chosen items
Signed code only; restricted dynamic loading
Walls serve security and platform control alike

title: Docker Security Model
description: Docker’s security model is namespace isolation plus configuration discipline. By default a container gets its own process, network, mount, and hostname namespaces — processes inside cannot see host processes — plus cgroup resource limits and a default seccomp profile blocking dangerous syscalls. The critical hardening steps are well documented: never run containers as root inside (map to unprivileged users via user namespaces), mount filesystems read-only where possible, drop unneeded capabilities (the default set is broader than most apps need), and never mount the Docker socket inside a container (socket access equals host root). Image hygiene matters equally: minimal base images, pinned digests, scanned for CVEs, rebuilt regularly. Orchestrators add policy layers — Kubernetes pod security standards, admission controllers — enforcing the hardening fleet-wide. The honest summary: Docker’s defaults are a development convenience; production security is the hardening checklist applied consistently.
key_points: Namespaces plus cgroups plus seccomp by default
Never root inside; read-only mounts; drop capabilities
Never mount the Docker socket in a container
Image hygiene: minimal, pinned, scanned, rebuilt

title: gVisor: The User-Space Kernel
description: gVisor, Google’s open-source project, strengthens container isolation by interposing a user-space kernel between the application and the host. Container syscalls are intercepted by the Sentry process, which implements Linux ABI semantics in Go — the application believes it is talking to Linux, while the host kernel sees only the Sentry’s narrow, filtered syscall stream. A container escape must therefore defeat two layers: the Sentry’s implementation and then the host — substantially raising the bar over namespace-only isolation. The cost is compatibility and performance: some syscalls and workloads (heavy ioctl users, certain networking patterns) run slower or need allowlisting, and the Sentry’s Linux reimplementation must track kernel behavior. Google runs gVisor in production for multi-tenant workloads (Cloud Run, App Engine) where tenants are mutually untrusted. The design lesson: when the shared kernel is the weak boundary, emulate the kernel rather than sharing it.
key_points: Sentry intercepts syscalls; implements Linux ABI in user space
Escape must beat two layers, not one
Cost: compatibility gaps and performance overhead
Production-proven for mutually untrusted tenants

title: Kata Containers: VM-Grade Isolation
description: Kata Containers give each container (or pod) its own lightweight virtual machine — hardware-enforced isolation with container UX. Each pod boots a minimal guest kernel in a QEMU-backed micro-VM; the container runtime inside thinks it is ordinary Docker, while the host sees only VM boundaries enforced by the CPU’s virtualization extensions. A kernel exploit inside the container escapes to the guest kernel, not the host — the hardware boundary holds where the shared-kernel boundary would not. Boot times are sub-second with optimized images, and memory overhead is modest per pod. The trade-offs: slightly higher resource use than namespaces, and reduced visibility for host-side monitoring tools. Kata shines where tenants are untrusted and the workload is container-shaped — public CI runners, serverless platforms, and regulated multi-tenancy. The trajectory it represents: the industry converging on hardware-rooted isolation as the standard for untrusted code, with pure namespaces reserved for trusted-internal workloads.
key_points: Each pod in its own lightweight VM; hardware-enforced boundary
Kernel exploit escapes to guest, not host
Sub-second boot; container UX preserved
For untrusted tenants: CI runners, serverless, regulated hosting

title: Antivirus and EDR Sandboxes
description: Security products run their own sandboxes to detonate the suspicious safely. Traditional antivirus sandboxes execute unknown files in instrumented VMs, watching for malicious behaviors — process injection, persistence mechanisms, network callbacks — and convicting on behavior rather than signatures. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) extends this to the live endpoint: suspicious processes get contained (network quarantined, filesystem fenced) while analysts investigate. Email gateways detonate attachments in cloud sandboxes before delivery, rewriting URLs to pass through detonation proxies. The arms race is active: modern malware fingerprints sandbox environments (timing checks, human-interaction checks, hardware tells) and sleeps through analysis — so vendors moved to bare-metal analysis, varied environments, and extended detonation windows. The enterprise lesson: detection sandboxes are a layer, not a verdict — detonation results feed the SOC’s judgment, and the determined adversary assumes the sandbox exists.
key_points: Detonation VMs convict on behavior, not signatures
EDR contains suspicious processes live on endpoints
Malware fingerprints sandboxes; vendors use bare metal
Detonation feeds analyst judgment — a layer, not a verdict

title: Enterprise Browser Isolation
description: Enterprise browser isolation moves the browser sandbox off the endpoint entirely: web pages render in a disposable cloud container, and the user’s device receives only pixels (or a sanitized DOM) — no web code ever executes on the endpoint. The security gain is structural: browser exploits, drive-by downloads, and malicious scripts detonate in the cloud container, which is destroyed after the session. The costs are latency (every interaction round-trips), fidelity (some web apps behave oddly through the pixel stream), and infrastructure (rendering farms are not free). Vendors split between pixel-streaming (maximum isolation, heaviest) and DOM-sanitizing (lighter, some code reaches the endpoint after cleaning). Adoption concentrates where the threat justifies it: finance, government, and organizations with high-value targets and low tolerance for endpoint compromise. The model’s honesty: it concedes the endpoint browser cannot be made safe enough, and moves the risk where it can be contained and discarded.
key_points: Pages render in cloud containers; endpoint gets pixels
No web code executes on the user device
Costs: latency, fidelity quirks, infrastructure
For high-value targets with low compromise tolerance

title: Seccomp: The Syscall Filter
description: Seccomp-bpf is the Linux kernel’s programmable sandbox primitive: a Berkeley Packet Filter program attached to a process that decides, per syscall, whether to allow, deny, or trap. Chrome’s renderer, Docker’s default profile, OpenSSH’s privilege-separated children, and systemd services all use seccomp to shrink the kernel attack surface — a compromised process that can only call read, write, and exit cannot reach the vulnerable ioctl that would have been its escape. Writing filters is the discipline: allowlist the syscalls the program legitimately needs (traced via strace during testing), deny the rest, and handle the architecture-specific syscall numbers. The failure mode is over-permissiveness — a filter allowing the dangerous calls it was meant to block — which is why generated profiles (from tools like oci-seccomp-bpf recorders) beat hand-written ones. Seccomp is the reason modern sandboxes can promise “even exploited, the process cannot reach the kernel’s dangerous corners” — the filter is the wall’s foundation.
key_points: BPF program decides per-syscall: allow, deny, trap
Shrinks kernel attack surface for compromised processes
Allowlist via traced legitimate syscalls; deny the rest
Generated profiles beat hand-written for correctness

title: Linux Namespaces: The Isolation Building Blocks
description: Linux namespaces are the kernel feature that makes containers possible: they partition global system resources so a group of processes sees only its own slice. Seven namespace types exist — mount (filesystem view), PID (process IDs), network (interfaces, routes), IPC, UTS (hostname), user (UID mapping), and cgroup — and combining them builds the container’s private world. A container’s PID 1 is just an ordinary process on the host; the namespace makes it believe it is init. User namespaces are the security keystone: they map the container’s root (UID 0) to an unprivileged host UID, so a container-root breakout still faces an unprivileged host user. Namespaces compose with cgroups (resource limits) and seccomp (syscall filters) into the full isolation stack. Understanding namespaces matters because every container escape is a namespace failure — the breakout that reaches the host’s mount namespace owns the host’s filesystem view. The primitives are simple; the composition is the engineering.
key_points: Seven types partition processes, mounts, network, users
Container PID 1 is an ordinary host process
User namespaces map container root to unprivileged host UID
Every container escape is a namespace failure

details.types: mount, PID, net, IPC, UTS, user, cgroup

t: Linux Namespaces: The Isolation Building Blocks

title: Capability Dropping in Containers
description: Linux capabilities split root’s power into 40-plus separate privileges, and dropping the unneeded ones is core container hardening. A container that only serves HTTP needs no CAP_SYS_ADMIN, no CAP_NET_RAW, no CAP_SYS_PTRACE — yet Docker’s default capability set historically included several dangerous ones for compatibility. The hardening workflow: start from the minimal set (often just CHOWN, SETUID, SETGID for file handling), test the workload, and add back only what breaks — documented per capability. Dropped capabilities are enforced by the kernel regardless of UID: even a process running as root inside the container cannot use a dropped capability. Orchestrators now enforce this fleet-wide — Kubernetes pod security standards require dropping ALL and adding back selectively. The principle generalizes beyond containers: every sandboxed process should hold the least privilege its function needs, because the capability the attacker cannot use is the exploit that fails.
key_points: 40+ capabilities split root’s power
Drop ALL, add back only what breaks
Kernel-enforced regardless of container UID
Least privilege: the unusable capability is the failed exploit

title: Read-Only Containers
description: Running containers with read-only root filesystems is one of the highest-value hardening steps: it converts entire exploit classes from “persistent compromise” to “failed write.” Malware that cannot write cannot install persistence, modify binaries, or drop cron jobs — the read-only mount denies it at the kernel. Legitimate write needs are served explicitly: tmpfs mounts for scratch space, named volumes for data, each declared in the container spec so the writable surface is audited. Applications sometimes resist — legacy apps that write logs or temp files to their install directory — and the fix is redirecting those paths to volumes, which usually improves the app’s hygiene anyway. Combined with non-root users and dropped capabilities, read-only filesystems make the container’s post-exploitation landscape barren: the attacker gets a shell with nowhere to write and nothing privileged to call. Orchestrators can enforce it cluster-wide as admission policy.
key_points: Read-only root: exploits fail at the write
No persistence, no binary modification, no cron drops
Write needs served via declared tmpfs and volumes
Enforceable cluster-wide as admission policy

title: macOS Seatbelt Profiles
description: Seatbelt is macOS’s mandatory-access-control sandboxing framework — the engine behind every App Store app sandbox, Safari tab isolation, and system daemon confinement. A seatbelt profile is a Scheme-like policy listing exactly what the process may do: which files it can read or write (by path pattern), which Mach services it can talk to, which network operations are allowed — everything else denied by default. Profiles compile to kernel-enforced policy; the sandboxed process cannot escalate past them regardless of its UID. Developers meet seatbelt through entitlements (the high-level capability declarations) while the system translates them into profile rules. Debugging sandbox denials is a learned skill: the Console’s sandboxd messages name the denied operation, and the fix is either a missing entitlement or a legitimate access the profile must allow. Seatbelt’s lesson for sandbox design: default-deny with explicit allows is the only policy shape that survives contact with attackers — allowlists age well, denylists do not.
key_points: Scheme-like policies: explicit allows, default deny
Kernel-enforced regardless of UID
Entitlements are the developer-facing layer
Allowlists age well; denylists do not

title: Systemd Sandboxing for Services
description: Systemd turned every Linux service into a sandboxing opportunity: unit files declare per-service restrictions the kernel enforces. ProtectSystem=strict mounts the filesystem read-only for the service; ProtectHome=yes hides home directories; PrivateTmp gives the service its own /tmp invisible to others; NoNewPrivileges blocks privilege escalation; SystemCallFilter applies seccomp allowlists — each a one-line declaration. A web service unit with these five lines runs confined even if the daemon has a remote exploit: the attacker’s shell cannot write the filesystem, read homes, see other tmp files, escalate, or call dangerous syscalls. The incremental model is the win: harden one service per maintenance window, test, and move on — no flag day, no re-architecture. Systemd’s sandboxing is the most deployed application sandboxing on earth by service count, precisely because it asks so little: a few unit-file lines between every daemon and the system it serves.
key_points: Per-service kernel restrictions as unit-file lines
Read-only system, hidden homes, private tmp, no escalation
Compromised daemon stays confined
Incremental: harden one service per window

title: The Sandbox as Security Boundary: Limits
description: Honest sandbox engineering names the limits: sandboxes are probabilistic defenses, not proofs. Kernel exploits pierce every software sandbox on the host — the entire model assumes the kernel holds, which is why kernel hardening and rapid patching are part of every sandbox story. Side channels (Spectre, Meltdown, and their descendants) read across isolation the hardware never promised to provide; mitigations are partial and costly. The broker problem: sandboxes need privileged helpers (the broker, the portal, the daemon), and every helper is attack surface — the history of sandbox escapes is largely the history of broker bugs. Human factors bound the rest: users grant the permissions the sandbox asks about, click through the warnings, and install the profile that defeats the model. The mature posture treats the sandbox as one layer in depth: sandbox plus patching plus least privilege plus monitoring plus user training. The sandbox that promises total safety is selling something; the sandbox that promises raised attacker cost is engineering.
key_points: Kernel exploits pierce every software sandbox on the host
Side channels read across hardware-unpromised isolation
Brokers are attack surface: escape history is broker-bug history
One layer in depth — never the whole posture
t: The Sandbox as Security Boundary: Limits

title: Choosing a Sandboxing Strategy
description: Choosing sandboxing starts with the threat model, not the tool catalog. Untrusted code from the internet (browsers, email attachments): browser sandboxes plus disposable VMs for detonation — the code never earns trust. Third-party applications on endpoints: OS app sandboxes (macOS/iOS/Android models, Flatpak/Snap/Firejail on Linux) — containment by default, portals for access. Server workloads: containers hardened (non-root, read-only, dropped caps, seccomp) for trusted-internal, gVisor or Kata for untrusted tenants — match the boundary strength to tenant trust. Regulated data: Qubes-style compartmentalization or enterprise browser isolation where the data’s value justifies the friction. The selection discipline: name the adversary, name what they win by escaping, and spend proportionally — the startup’s blog container does not need Kata, and the dissident’s laptop is not safe with default Docker. Review yearly: threats evolve, primitives improve, and last year’s adequate is this year’s gap.
key_points: Start from threat model, not tool catalog
Internet code: browser sandbox plus disposable VM
Servers: hardened containers; gVisor/Kata for untrusted tenants
Spend proportionally; review yearly

title: Sandbox Monitoring and Escape Detection
description: Sandboxes need watching because escapes are silent: the monitoring stack looks for the signs that containment failed. Behavioral signals: a sandboxed process spawning unexpected children, touching files outside its profile, or making syscalls its filter should have blocked — each a containment violation worth an alert. Integrity signals: hash the sandbox’s policy and binaries, and alert on changes — the profile edit that quietly widened access is the classic precursor. Network signals: the sandbox that suddenly talks to new destinations is either compromised or misconfigured; either way it needs eyes. The response playbook is pre-written: isolate the host, snapshot the sandbox state for forensics, compare against the known-good policy, and rebuild from clean images — never “clean” a suspected escape in place. Red teams test the monitoring by attempting escapes on schedule; the drill that finds the blind spot is cheaper than the incident that does. Monitored sandboxes contain; unmonitored sandboxes merely hope.
key_points: Watch for containment violations: children, files, syscalls
Hash policies and binaries; alert on changes
New network destinations mean compromise or misconfiguration
Pre-written playbook: isolate, snapshot, rebuild clean
